front_blocks.md: Why are Group I metals called the alkali metals?

back_blocks.md: They are called alkali metals because they react with water to form **alkaline solutions** with a high pH.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Reactivity of Group I metals decreases as you go down the group.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Reactivity of Group I metals **increases** going down the group, so potassium reacts more vigorously with water than lithium.

front_blocks.md: Why are Group I metals stored under oil?

back_blocks.md: Group I metals are stored under oil to prevent them from reacting with **oxygen and water vapour** in the air.

front_blocks.md: What is the distinguishing observation when potassium reacts with water, compared with sodium?

back_blocks.md: Potassium reacts more vigorously than sodium and burns with a **lilac flame** on the surface of the water.

front_blocks.md: Why does reactivity increase going down Group I?

back_blocks.md: Reactivity increases because the **outer electron** is further from the nucleus in each successive element, so it is **more easily lost** when the metal reacts.

back_blocks.md: **Diatomic** means consisting of two atoms bonded together. All halogens exist as diatomic molecules, e.g. Cl<sub>2</sub>, Br<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub>.

Reactivity of Group VII elements increases going down the group.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Reactivity of Group VII elements **decreases** going down the group, because the outer shell is further from the nucleus and harder to attract an incoming electron.

front_blocks.md: Why does reactivity decrease going down Group VII?

back_blocks.md: Going down Group VII, the **atomic radius** increases and there is greater **electron shielding**, so the nucleus attracts an incoming electron less strongly and it becomes harder to gain the outer electron needed to react.

back_blocks.md: All Group VII elements are diatomic: **F**<sub>**2**</sub> (fluorine), **Cl**<sub>**2**</sub> (chlorine), **Br**<sub>**2**</sub> (bromine) and **I**<sub>**2**</sub> (iodine).

front_blocks.md: How is a **halide ion** formed from a halogen atom?

back_blocks.md: A halide ion is formed when a halogen atom **gains one electron** to complete its outer shell of eight electrons, giving it a **1−** charge.

front_blocks.md: What is a halogen displacement reaction?

back_blocks.md: A halogen displacement reaction is one in which a **more reactive halogen** displaces a **less reactive halogen** from an aqueous solution of its halide salt.

cards.front_md: What is a halogen displacement reaction?
cards.back_md: A halogen displacement reaction is one in which a **more reactive halogen** displaces a **less reactive halogen** from an aqueous solution of its halide salt.

front_blocks.md: When Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) is added to KBr (aq), the solution turns **..........** because **..........** is displaced.

back_blocks.md: When Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) is added to KBr (aq), the solution turns **orange** because **bromine** is displaced.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Iodine can displace bromine from a solution of potassium bromide.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Iodine is **less reactive** than bromine, so it cannot displace bromine. Only a more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive one.

front_blocks.md: Why can chlorine displace bromide ions from solution?

back_blocks.md: Chlorine is **more reactive** than bromine so it can **oxidise** bromide ions, gaining electrons to form chloride ions and releasing bromine.

front_blocks.md: What colour change is observed when bromine solution is added to potassium iodide solution, and what does this indicate?

back_blocks.md: The solution turns **brown**, indicating that bromine has displaced iodide ions to form **iodine**, I<sub>2</sub>, which is more reactive than iodine.

cards.front_md: What colour change is observed when bromine solution is added to potassium iodide solution, and what does this indicate?
cards.back_md: The solution turns **brown**, indicating that bromine has displaced iodide ions to form **iodine**, I<sub>2</sub>, which is more reactive than iodine.

front_blocks.md: How does reactivity order of chlorine, bromine and iodine determine the outcome of a displacement reaction?

back_blocks.md: **Chlorine** is the most reactive and **iodine** the least. A halogen will only displace a halide ion that is lower in reactivity, so chlorine displaces both bromide and iodide while bromine only displaces iodide.

front_blocks.md: Where are the transition elements found in the Periodic Table?

front_blocks.md: What two oxidation states does iron commonly form, and what is the significance of transition elements having variable oxidation states?

back_blocks.md: Iron forms **Fe**<sup>**2+**</sup> and **Fe**<sup>**3+**</sup> ions. **Variable oxidation states** are a key property of transition elements and distinguish them from most other metals.

front_blocks.md: Why are transition elements widely used as industrial catalysts?

back_blocks.md: Transition elements are effective catalysts because they can form ions with **variable oxidation states**, allowing them to accept and donate electrons during a reaction.

front_blocks.md: Why are scandium and zinc not classed as transition elements, despite being in the transition element region of the table?

back_blocks.md: Scandium and zinc are not classed as transition elements because they do not form **coloured compounds** and each has only **one oxidation state**.

front_blocks.md: Why are the noble gases described as inert?

back_blocks.md: Noble gases are inert because they have **full outer shells** of electrons, making their electronic configurations extremely stable and leaving no tendency to gain or lose electrons.

back_blocks.md: Helium has the electronic configuration **2** and neon has the configuration **2,8**, both giving a full outer shell.

front_blocks.md: Why do noble gases not form bonds with other elements?

back_blocks.md: Noble gases do not form bonds because their **outer shells are already full**, so they have no need to gain or lose electrons to achieve stability.

front_blocks.md: How many electrons does argon have in its outer shell, and how does this explain its lack of reactivity?

back_blocks.md: Argon has **8 electrons** in its outer shell. This **full outer shell** means argon has no tendency to gain or lose electrons, so it does not react.
